intro: Thais are forgiving of visitors who do not know the customs — but a little awareness earns a warmer welcome and helps you avoid the things locals find uncomfortable.

blocks.html: Short answer: The heart of Thai etiquette is respect and politeness. Greet with a wai or a smile, dress modestly at temples, take off your shoes before entering homes and some shops, never touch someone’s head, and don’t point with your feet. Above all, always show respect for the monarchy and religion.

blocks.title: About the monarchy
blocks.html: Thais hold the monarchy in very high regard, and it is protected by strict laws. Avoid any negative comments or gestures about it entirely, and stand respectfully when the royal anthem plays in cinemas or public spaces.

faq.q: What is the wai, and do I have to do it?
faq.a: The wai is a palms-together gesture of respect. Tourists don’t need to wai everyone, but returning a wai or smiling and nodding when someone wais you is polite. Generally the younger or junior person wais first.

faq.q: How should I dress to enter a temple?
faq.a: Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees for both men and women — no tank tops, short shorts or tight outfits. Some temples lend cover-ups, and you must remove your shoes before entering the hall.

faq.q: Why are the head and feet such a big deal?
faq.a: In Thai culture the head is the highest, most sacred part of the body and the feet the lowest. Touching someone’s head or pointing/nudging things with your feet is considered rude, so avoid both.

quickAnswerHtml: Thai etiquette centers on respect and politeness. Greet with a wai or smile, dress modestly covering shoulders and knees at temples, and remove your shoes in homes and temples. Never touch someone's head or point with your feet. Above all, always show respect for the monarchy and Buddhism — these matter deeply to locals.
